description: AgroVision is a team of passionate innovators dedicated to transforming agriculture through technology, data science, and satellite observations. Our mission is to leverage NASA's Earth observation data to help farmers make smarter decisions
summary: AgroVision is a mobile-first web app that helps small and mid-size farmers in the Dominican Republic decide what to plant next. The farmer marks the field on a satellite map, says what was planted last, whether there is irrigation and what the soil looks like, and AgroVision compares 22 common Dominican crops across four pillars: water, drought, pests and price. It combines NASA POWER climate data and NASA GIBS satellite layers with FAO, IDIAF and Ministry of Agriculture references, and answers in plain language (English or Spanish) with star ratings, a short "why this crop and not another", a 7-day rain alert, a profit range and the source behind every point. It addresses Field Shift by turning NASA Earth observation data into a crop-rotation decision a farmer can understand and discuss with a technician. It matters because most Dominican farmers decide by habit or by last season's price, without access to climate, rotation or market evidence; AgroVision puts that evidence in their pocket, by voice and on WhatsApp, and it also works with weak or no signal.
details:
What it does

AgroVision answers one question for a farmer: "What should I plant next on this field, and why?"

• Mark the farm: on a satellite map the farmer taps 50 m grid cells, picks satellite-detected approximate parcels, or draws a polygon. The area is shown in tareas (the local unit) and hectares. Farms are saved on the phone, and each one gets its own advice.

• Tell it about the field: last crop, irrigation (yes / rain-fed / not sure), soil texture (sandy, mixed, clay) and soil color.

• Recommendation: the best option with 1–5 stars, plus alternatives, scored on four pillars: crop water needs (FAO-56), drought in the province (FAO GIEWS), pest and rotation rules (IDIAF/CEDAF catalog) and the wholesale price at harvest time (Ministry of Agriculture).

• "Why this crop?": a plain-language explanation of why it is the pick, why not the others, what the rotation does for the soil (for example, maize after beans uses the nitrogen the legume leaves), which pests to watch, and what the app does not know.

• Extra tools: a 7-day rain alert per farm ("don't irrigate Thursday, rain is coming"), a profit range ("how much will I make?") and an oversupply warning when national sowing is well above previous years.

• Voice and sharing: a voice assistant that knows the farm and answers with sources, sharing to WhatsApp, and offline use with data cached on the phone.

How it works

• Next.js app with a MapLibre map.

• NASA POWER monthly climatology and recent daily data for the farm's coordinates, plus NASA GIBS layers (MODIS NDVI, GPM IMERG precipitation, SMAP soil moisture) for visual context.

• A rules engine scores the four pillars from cited sources, and every number links to its source in a "Where does this come from?" panel.

• Costs come from the Ministry of Agriculture 2019 production-cost sheets, updated with the Central Bank (BCRD) CPI.

• Prices come from the Ministry's official wholesale series (2017–2026).

• Approximate parcels were segmented with MobileSAM on Esri imagery and filtered with ESA WorldCover 2021.

• A service worker keeps the app usable offline.

Benefits

• Turns scattered public data into one clear, sourced decision.

• Speaks the farmer's language: plain words in Spanish or English, tareas, and stars instead of formulas.

• Encourages crop rotation that protects the soil and breaks pest cycles.

• Is honest about uncertainty: it says what it doesn't know, never invents numbers, and is decision support, not a guarantee. Wholesale prices are a Santo Domingo reference, not farm-gate prices, and parcels are approximate, not cadastral.

What we hope to achieve

• A free basic tier for every Dominican farmer, funded by an institution.

• Validation with farmers and agronomists in the San Juan valley.

• Later: soil sensors for larger farms and cooperatives, and zone dashboards for lenders, insurers and agricultural agencies.

Tools

• Language and frameworks: TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, MapLibre GL, Zod and lucide-react.

• AI and data: Vercel AI SDK and AI Gateway for the voice and text assistant, libSQL/Turso, and Python for data pipelines.

• Testing: Node test runner, Playwright end-to-end tests and axe-core accessibility checks.

• Hosting: deployed on Vercel.

Source code: https://github.com/fraineralex/agrovision-spaceapps-2026

The interface is available in English and Spanish (language selector), because its users are Dominican farmers. The demo video has an English voice-over and English subtitles.

Use of AI (disclosure)

Yes. AI was a tool to build faster; the idea, data choices and decisions are the team's.

Assistants used to build the project (all logged in AI_USAGE.md):

• OpenAI Codex: project setup, data pipelines (prices, NASA POWER cache, Sentinel-2 parcels), voice, offline architecture and documentation.

• Anthropic Claude (Claude Pro and Claude Code): research and writing; the crop advisor in plain language; soil and pest sections; tests; the English README introduction; this submission text; the demo video and pitch deck.

• Antigravity (Gemini / Claude) with Impeccable: tab navigation, visual design, accessibility and compact layouts.

• Cursor agent: water and climate pillars, and a prototype of the RAG vector search.

• Grok (xAI): early satellite map layers and territorial visualization.

• OpenAI GPT-6 / ImageGen: lazy loading, light and dark themes, and enhancement of a CC0 photo. The photo is labeled "AI-enhanced image" in the app.

AI inside the app:

• Voice assistant: OpenAI gpt-realtime-mini via Vercel AI Gateway.

• Text answers: Anthropic Claude Haiku 5.5 via Vercel AI Gateway.

• Embeddings for guide search: Google Gemini embedding models. An optional local model (Qwen3-1.7B through llama.cpp) can be used instead.

• The assistant is told to answer only from the app's sourced data and to say when there is no source.

• MobileSAM was used to segment approximate field outlines.

Demo video:

• The voice-over is AI-generated (Kokoro-82M TTS). It is disclosed here and in the video file metadata.

• The motion graphics and the recreated aerial image were coded with AI assistance, and the video carries a visible "Made with AI assistance · AI voice" watermark.

• No NASA logos or branding were generated or modified.
